en: Abhidharmakośa-kārikā, composed by the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu of the Sarvāstivāda school;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by imperial decree.
I pay homage to the Teacher who, through every mode, has extinguished all darkness and pulled sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death; I shall now expound the Abhidharmakośa Śāstra.
The Abhidharma is defined as pure wisdom along with its attendants, as well as the wisdoms and treatises that lead to its attainment;
because it summarizes that ultimate truth and relies upon it, this work is established under the name *Abhidharmakośa*.
Apart from the analytical discernment of phenomena, there is truly no other superior means capable of extinguishing all afflictions;
because of these afflictions, the world drifts in the ocean of existence—therefore, it is said that the Buddha taught the Abhidharma.

Regarding tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena: with the exception of the Path, all other conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena are called "tainted" because the outflows increase therein.
The untainted refers to the Truth of the Path and the three kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
These are space and the two types of cessation; among these, space is non-obstruction.
Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is disjunction (visamyoga); it is distinct for each object of bondage.
The absolute obstruction of that which is to arise is the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena— namely the five aggregates such as form—
are also called "paths of the world," "bases of expression," "possessing departure," and "possessing objects.
Those that are with outflows are called "aggregates of clinging" and are also said to be "with contention."
As well as suffering, its origin, the world, the bases of views, and the three realms of existence;
matter consists solely of the five faculties, the five objects, and the unmanifest.
That which is the support for their consciousnesses, consisting of translucent matter, is called the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
Visible form consists of two or twenty types; sound has only eight kinds;
taste has six and fragrance four; touch has eleven as its nature.
Whether the mind is distracted or absent, and whether they flow as pure or impure, [these are the characteristics of the sense objects].
The nature of being derived from the great elements is what is called "unmanifest" (avijñapti) by this [definition].
The great elements refer to the four realms: namely, earth, water, fire, and wind;
they perform the functions of supporting and so forth, and possess the natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion.
"Earth refers to visible form and shape; names are established according to worldly convention.
Water and fire are likewise, and wind is both an element and so too.
Herein, the faculties and their objects are explained as the ten bases and elements."
Feeling has the nature of experiencing; perception has the nature of grasping images.

The four remaining aggregates are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Thus, these three—feeling and the others—along with unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are named the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Consciousness (vijñāna) refers to the individual discernment [of objects]; this is what is called the sense base of mind (manāyatana), and it should be understood as the seven elements (dhātus). It is because the six bodies of consciousness, having ceased immediately prior, become the mind.
Thus, by means of the six groups of consciousness themselves, that which has just ceased constitutes the mind.
Because it establishes the sixth basis, one should know that the eighteen elements (dhātus) exist.
They collectively encompass all phenomena (dharma) through the single categories of aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements;
they include their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and nothing else, because they are devoid of the nature of others.
Because their types, objects, and consciousnesses are identical, although the substance of the two [eyes] is one,
they each arise as two for the sake of symmetry. Aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*),
and elements (*dhātu*) are defined by their meanings as "accumulations," "gateways for arising," and "lineages," respectively.
Because of the three types of delusion, faculties, and inclinations, the aggregates, bases, and elements are taught as triads.
Because they are the roots of contention, the causes of birth and death, and for the sake of establishing the proper order,
feeling and perception are established as distinct aggregates among the mental factors.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not included among the aggregates (*skandha*), because its meaning is incompatible [with their definition].
They are established in their sequential order according to their coarseness, defilement, being like a vessel, and so forth, as well as their distinct realms (*dhātu*).
Of the first five [objects], only the present exists; four of these objects consist solely of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
The remaining [bases] are distinguished by their functions being distant, rapid, and clear, or by their order according to location;
because they are most excellent in their differentiation and encompass many superior phenomena,
one location is named "form" (rūpa) and one is named the "base of phenomena" (dharmāyatana).
The Muni taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma;
their essence is either speech or names, and they are thus subsumed within the aggregates of form or formations.
Others say that the measure of the aggregates of Dharma is as stated in that treatise.
Or, following the discourse on the aggregates and so forth, one practices the antidotes according to reality.
Likewise, the remaining aggregates and so forth are each subsumed within what has been previously explained as appropriate; one should carefully examine their specific characteristics.
The space element refers to apertures; tradition says it is light and darkness.
The consciousness element consists of contaminated consciousness, which is the basis for the birth of sentient beings.
One [element] is visible, namely form; ten [elements] are material and possess resistance.
Excluding form and sound, these eight are indeterminate; the remaining three are of all three types.

Eighteen are bound to the desire realm; fourteen are bound to the form realm, excluding the two [objects] of odor and taste and the two consciousnesses; the last three are bound to the formless realm.
The mind, mental objects, and mental consciousness are common to both [the outflow-free and the outflow-tainted]; the remaining [faculties] are exclusively outflow-tainted.
The five consciousnesses possess only vitarka and vicāra; for the last three [consciousnesses], all three are present, while for the rest, none exist.
It is said that the five [sensory] consciousnesses are non-conceptual, because they lack the conceptualization of calculation and the recollection of memory.
The wisdom that is discursive on the mental level has the various mental attentions as its substance.
Seven of the mental factors and half of the dharma-element possess objects; the remainder do not.
The first eight elements and sound are non-appropriated; the rest are of both kinds.
Within the element of tangibility there are two [types]; the remaining nine are derived from matter (*rūpa-nirmita*).
The same applies to one portion of the dharma-element. Ten material elements are accumulative.
That is to say, only the four external elements can both cut and be cut.
They are both that which is burned and that which weighs; they are that which burns and that which is weighed.
Regarding the internal five [faculties], there are those born of maturation and those produced by nourishment; sound is not born of maturation.
Eight [elements] are of the nature of outflow; they are also of the nature of being born of maturation.
The remaining three [realms] consist only of dharmas; the last three exist only momentarily.
The eye and the eye-consciousness element may be acquired either independently or together, and they are not equal.
The twelve internal [realms], such as the eye, and the six external ones, such as form, [are established].
Dharmas are of three types: those with a commonality of nature (*sabhāga*), and the other two. They perform their own functions, whether active or inactive.
Fifteen [factors] are abandoned only through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); the last three realms are common to all three [types of abandonment].
Those that are non-defiled are not born from the six [consciousnesses]; in the form realm, they are certainly not abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*).
A portion of the eye and the dharma-element are said to be the eight kinds of seeing;
the wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not seeing, because it does not judge.
It is the eye, when functioning as a homogeneous basis, that sees forms, not the consciousness that depends upon it.
It is traditionally taught that [the eye] cannot perceive [objects] because it is obstructed by intervening forms;
or rather, because when both eyes function simultaneously, the perception of form is distinct.
Thus, the sense organs of the eye, ear, and mind, along with their respective objects, are characterized by the three [features of] non-arrival.
It should be known that the three [faculties] beginning with the nose perceive objects of equal magnitude;
the latter [mental consciousness] relies solely on the past, while the five consciousnesses rely on [the faculty] either simultaneously or subsequently.
Because the consciousness varies according to the transformation of the sense organ, the eye and so forth are termed "bases" (āśraya).
Because of those [factors] and because of the unique cause (*asādhāraṇa-hetu*), consciousness is designated according to its faculty.
The eye is not inferior to the body; visual consciousness is not superior to the eye.
For color-form, it is so in relation to all consciousnesses; for both [the eye and color-form], it is likewise in relation to the body.
As it is with the eye, so it is with the ear; the next three [faculties] belong to their own level.
The body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower level; it should be known that the mind-faculty is not fixed.
The five external objects are cognized by two [consciousnesses]; the eternal dharma-realm is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
One portion of the dharmas is faculties, as are the twelve internal bases.
It is traditionally taught that five [faculties] have predominance over four [objects], and the four [sexual] faculties have predominance over two kinds [of objects].
Among the defiled and the pure, five and eight [faculties] each act as predominant factors in their respective categories.
Because they exercise sovereignty over their respective objects, the six faculties are established in total.
From among these, two faculties are established from the body, because they exercise sovereignty over femininity and masculinity.
Because they exercise sovereignty over coexistence, defilement, and purification, [the remaining faculties are established].
One should know that life, the five feelings, faith and the others are established as faculties;

so too are the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known," which possess sovereignty over the attainment of successive paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth.
Because the mind’s basis, its differentiation, its abiding, its defilement, its equipment,
and its purification are established by these measures, they are designated as faculties (*indriya*). Alternatively,
they are the basis for the process of transmigration, as well as for birth, abiding, and experience.
The first fourteen [factors] are established in this way; the same applies to their cessation.
That which is dissatisfaction of the body is called suffering (*duḥkha*); that very same satisfaction is called pleasure (*sukha*).
Furthermore, the mental satisfaction of the three dhyānas is likewise [pleasure], while in other stages it is termed joy (*prīti*).
Displeasure of mind is called *daurmanasya* (sorrow); the intermediate state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is undifferentiated from the two [preceding states].
The three faculties are established based on the nine paths: those of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning.
Only the last three are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*); the others include the material faculties, life, sorrow, and suffering.

One should know that only [the faculty of] outflows (āsrava) is exclusively [defiled]; the two [faculties of pleasure and equanimity] and the remaining nine faculties pertain to both [the defiled and the undefiled].
The life-faculty is exclusively maturation (vipāka); the faculty of grief and the final eight are not.
The faculties of form, mind, and the four sensations each pertain to both.
Sorrow definitely has a ripening result; the first eight and the last three do not.
The mental faculty and the remaining faculties—feeling and so forth—each pertain to both [types of results].
Only the last eight faculties are exclusively wholesome; sorrow pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The mind and the other sensations are of three types; the first eight are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Bound to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, they are respectively devoid of the last three [of each realm], as well as female and male faculties, sorrow and suffering, along with the remaining forms, joy, and pleasure.
The mental [faculty] and the three feelings are common to all three [types of abandonment]; sorrow is abandoned by insight and cultivation;
nine are abandoned only by cultivation; five are abandoned by cultivation, and neither by insight nor by nature.
Those born from desire, and those born from the womb, egg, or moisture, initially obtain two types of maturation.
Those born by transformation possess six, seven, or eight; in the form realm, six; above that (the formless realm), only life.
At the moment of death, the faculties cease: in the formless realm, three; in the form realm, eight;
in the desire realm, nineteen, eighteen, or eight all at once; or four gradually; for the wholesome, five are added.
Nine attain the two fruits of the extremes; seven, eight, or nine attain the two intermediate fruits;
eleven attain arhatship. Based on a single [moment], there can be such a teaching.
One who possesses life, mind, and equanimity necessarily possesses three [of these] each.
If one possesses the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), one necessarily possesses four;
if one possesses the eye-faculty and so forth, as well as the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), one necessarily possesses five faculties.
If one possesses the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), one necessarily possesses seven.
If female or male faculties, or sorrow, are acquired, faith and the others each acquire eight.
The two untainted minds acquire eleven; the first untainted mind acquires thirteen.
At the very minimum, eight are acquired when there is no wholesome [mind]: the faculties of sensation, body, life, and mind.
When a fool is born in the formless realm, they possess the wholesome [faculties], life, mind, and equanimity;
at most, they possess nineteen. Those with both sexual organs possess these minus the three pure faculties.
Noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire possess these minus the two pure faculties and one sexual organ.
In a subtle aggregate of desire that lacks sound, there are eight entities if no faculties are present;
if the body faculty is present, there are nine entities; if other faculties are present, there are ten entities.
Mind and mental factors necessarily coexist; so too do the various formations, their characteristics, or acquisitions.
Mental factors consist of five categories, distinguished as the universal ground-factors and so forth.
Sensation, perception, volition, contact, and desire; wisdom, mindfulness, and attention;
resolve and concentration—these are present in all states of mind.
Faith and heedfulness, pliancy, equanimity, shame and dread,
the two roots, non-harming, and diligence are found only in wholesome minds.
Delusion, heedlessness, laziness, lack of faith, lethargy, and restlessness are always and exclusively associated with defiled minds.
Only associated with all unwholesome minds,
anger, concealment, stinginess, envy, vexation, harmfulness, resentment, guile, deceit, and pride—
these categories are called the factors of the minor defilement ground.
Because desire possesses vitarka and vicāra, there are twenty-two mental factors; sometimes regret (kaukṛtya) is added.
In the case of unwholesome [minds] that are not shared, and when associated with views, there are only twenty.
The four afflictions, anger, and so forth, The twenty-one [mental factors] of regret, The eighteen [factors] associated with the obscured, And the twelve admitted for the unobscured.
Sleep is not incompatible with any; If present, it increases the total by one.
In the first dhyāna, unwholesome states, as well as regret and torpor, are eliminated.
In the middle dhyānas, vitarka is further eliminated. In the higher stages, vicāra and the rest are also eliminated.
Lack of shame and lack of dread consist in having no sense of gravity and seeing no fear in transgressions.
Affection and respect consist of faith and shame; they exist only in the realms of desire and form.
Vitarka and vicāra are the coarseness and subtlety of the mind. Pride is the inflation of the mind relative to others;
conceit arises from attachment to one's own qualities, a loftiness of mind that disregards all else.
Mind, thought, and consciousness are one in essence;
mind and mental factors have a basis, an object, and a mode of activity, and their association has five meanings.
The formations dissociated from mind are acquisition, non-acquisition, and homogeneity.
Non-conception, the two meditative attainments, and life-force; The [factors] of characteristics, names, and phrases, and so forth.
"Acquisition" (prāpti) refers to obtaining and possession; "Non-acquisition" (aprāpti) is the opposite of this.
Acquisition and non-acquisition exist only with respect to one's own continuum and the two types of cessation.
The dharmas of the three time periods each have three [types of acquisition]; those that are wholesome and so forth possess only wholesome and so forth [acquisitions].
Those with a specific realm of attachment have acquisitions belonging to their own realm; those without attachment have acquisitions that pervade all four realms.
Those that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner have three [types of acquisition]; those not to be abandoned through cultivation have two kinds.
The non-defined (avyākṛta) [dharmas] arise simultaneously [with their acquisition], excluding the two supernormal powers and transformations.
The obscured (nivṛta) material [dharmas] also arise simultaneously; in the desire and form realms, there is no prior arising.
Non-acquisition (aprāpti) is pure-non-defined (anivṛtāvyākṛta); for past and future [dharmas], there are three types each.
The non-possession (*aprāpti*) of the three paths of the noble ones belonging to the three realms is designated as the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*);
it is abandoned through the attainment of those dharmas or by changing one’s level (*bhūmi*).
Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) refers to the commonality among sentient beings; the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) exists within the realm of non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).

The cessation of mind and mental factors occurs in the state of the Unmanifested Attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), which is a ripening (*vipāka*) fruit residing in the Bṛhatphala heaven. This attainment is sought by those in the final dhyāna who seek liberation;
it is wholesome and results in feeling only in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*). It is not attained by noble ones (*ārya*), and when attained, it lasts for only one lifetime.
The attainment of cessation is likewise; it serves as a peaceful dwelling for those at the Peak of Existence.
It is wholesome, associated with two types of feeling, and indeterminate; it is acquired by the noble ones through preparatory effort.
One attains it upon becoming a Buddha, but not before, because of the thirty-four moments [of thought].
The two meditative attainments depend on the desire and form realms; the attainment of cessation first occurs among humans.
The essence of the life-faculty is longevity itself; it is able to sustain heat and consciousness.
Characteristics refer to the nature of all conditioned phenomena: arising, abiding, change, and cessation.
These [factors] such as "arising-of-arising" have efficacy regarding the eight and the one;
arising can give rise to that which is to arise, but not apart from the conjunction of causes and conditions.
What are called "name-bodies" (nāmakāya) and so forth are general designations for concepts, phrases, and syllables.
Sentient beings of the desire and form realms, Are of the nature of outflow and neutral.
The homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) is likewise, Along with the formless realm and maturation (*vipāka*).
Possession (*prāpti*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*) pertain to all three categories; Non-possession (*aprāpti*) is definitely of the nature of outflow.
The efficient cause, the co-existent, the similar, the associated, the pervasive, and the ripening—these six types of causes are accepted.
With the exception of itself, all other phenomena are the efficient cause; as for the co-existent, they are mutually effects of one another.
Just as the primary characteristics (lakṣaṇa) follow what is characterized (lakṣya), so too do the mind (citta), the mental factors (caitta),
the two types of discipline (saṃvara), their [respective] characteristics,
and the characteristics of the mind itself, all follow along with the mind. This is because they are equal in terms of time, fruit, goodness, and so forth.
The homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) is similar [to its effect]; it belongs to its own category (*nikāya*) and level (*bhūmi*), and is antecedent.
The Path (*mārga*) functions as a mutual cause across the nine levels, producing only equal or superior results.
The same applies to those produced through application (*prayoga*), such as those consisting of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*).
The associated cause is determined by the co-reliance of mind and mental factors.
The universal cause refers to those preceding [defilements] that act as the cause for defiled states within the same stage.
The ripening cause consists of the unwholesome, as well as the wholesome only when it is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Universal causes and similar-type causes have results in two time periods; the other three types have results in all three time periods.
The results are conditioned phenomena and disjunction; unconditioned phenomena have neither cause nor result.
The latter [result] is the ripening result; the former [cause] has the dominant result.
Of the same kind, pervasive, and outflowing; Arising together, associated, and of human effort.
Retribution is neutral dharmas; Belonging to sentient beings, produced by the determinate.
Outflow resembles its own cause; Disconnection is through the exhaustion [of defilements] by wisdom.
If it arises through the power of that [cause], this fruit is called "virile" (puruṣakāra-phala).
Excluding prior conditioned phenomena, all conditioned phenomena are "dominant fruits" (adhipati-phala).
Five [causes] take up their results only in the present; two [causes] likewise give their results in the present.
Past and present [dharmas] act as two causes; one [cause] acts only as a past cause.
Defiled dharmas and those born of maturation [act as causes] in this order; the remaining [dharmas], the first noble [dharmas], and the others follow respectively.
Excluding the maturation and pervasive [causes], and the two types of similar-class causes, the remaining [causes] produce future [dharmas].

This refers to the mind and mental factors; for all others, excluding those associated with them, it is said there are four kinds of conditions. The causal condition consists of the nature of five causes.
The equal-and-immediate condition is not subsequent; it refers to mind and mental factors that have already arisen.
All phenomena are the objects of perception (*ālambana*); the dominant condition (*adhipati*) is simply the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
Two causes function at the moment of ceasing; three causes function at the moment of arising.
The remaining two conditions operate in a manner contrary to these.
Mind and mental factors arise from four conditions; the two meditative attainments arise from three;
the rest arise from two conditions, because they are not produced by a creator god, nor sequentially, and so forth.
The great elements are the two causes for the great elements, and they are five kinds of causes for derived matter.
The conditioned consists of three types; for the unconditioned, there is only one cause.
In the desire realm, there are four minds: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
In the form and formless realms, the unwholesome is excluded. The untainted consists of two minds.
Wholesome [minds] of the desire realm arise from nine; these, in turn, arise from eight.
Defiled [minds] arise from ten and give rise to four; the remaining [neutral minds] arise from five and give rise to seven.
Wholesome [minds] of the form realm arise from eleven; these, in turn, arise from nine.
The obscured arises from eight; it in turn gives rise to six.
The unobscured arises from three; it in turn can give rise to six.
The wholesome of the formless realm gives rise to nine; it in turn arises from six.
The obscured arises from seven; the unobscured is as explained for the form realm.
The learner arises from four and produces five; the rest arise from five and produce four.
The twelve become twenty, namely the wholesome minds of the three realms.
When divided, those acquired through application and those acquired at birth, as well as the unobscured-neutral states of the desire realm, are each fourfold:
[the result of] maturation, the path of deportment, the sphere of craftsmanship, and the supernormal fruit.
In the form realm, the sphere of craftsmanship is excluded; the remaining numbers are as previously stated.
Within the defiled minds of the three realms, one obtains six, six, and two types [of knowledges];
in the wholesome mind of the form realm, three; and in the [wholesome] minds of training, four. All others are obtained by themselves.
As for those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and the six heavens of the desire realm:
The Desire Realm is said to consist of twenty [places], due to the distinctions among the hells and continents;
above this, seventeen locations are called the Form Realm.
Within it, there are three levels of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), each having three [stages], while the fourth meditative absorption has eight.
In the formless realm there is no location; it is fourfold according to birth.
By means of the homogeneous character (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), they cause the mind and its concomitants to continue in succession.
Among these, the hells and so forth are designated as the five destinies (*gati*) by their own names.
Only non-obscured and neutral; they belong to sentient beings and not to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Those with different bodies and different perceptions, those with different bodies and the same perception, the opposite of these (those with the same body and different perceptions), those with the same body and same perception, and the three lower formless realms—these are the [nine] abodes of beings.
Therefore, there are seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*); the others are not so because they involve impairment.

One should know that these, together with the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), constitute the nine abodes of sentient beings (*sattvāvāsa*); the rest are not places where beings delight to dwell.
The four stations of consciousness should be known as consisting solely of the four aggregates within their own respective realms;
consciousness alone is said not to be a station. These are subsumed under the four categories of the tainted (*sāsrava*).
Within them, there are four modes of birth; sentient beings are categorized as those born from eggs and so forth.

Humans and animals possess all four types of birth; those in the hells, as well as the various devas, and beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) are born only by transformation. Ghosts may be born either from a womb or by transformation.
Between the two states of death and birth, the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are termed the intermediate state.
Not having yet reached the place where one ought to go, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a [new] birth.
Like the continuity of grain and so forth, it arises in uninterrupted succession at its location.
Since a reflection is not established as being substantially real, it is not a valid analogy because of this inequality.
Two do not exist simultaneously in one place, nor do two arise through succession;
this is because the *gandharva* is taught [to exist] and because of the five and seven sūtras.
Since it is projected by a single karma, it possesses the form of its future existence.
The "fundamental existence" (pūrvakālabhava) refers to the period prior to death, occurring after the moment of birth.
It is visible to those with pure divine eyes; it possesses karmic supernormal powers, swift movement, and complete sense faculties.
It is non-obstructive, irreversible, feeds on odors, and does not endure for long.
With inverted minds they seek the realm of desire; those born from moisture or by transformation are stained by odors and locations.
The gods have their heads upward; the other three [humans, animals, and hungry ghosts] are horizontal; the denizens of hell have their heads turned downward. One enters the womb with full awareness;
two [animals and hungry ghosts] possess both [awareness at entry and abiding]; and three [humans, gods, and asuras] also possess awareness upon exiting.
In all stages, as well as in the egg, there is always a lack of awareness.

Regarding the first three types of entry into the womb—namely, those of the Wheel-turning King and the two kinds of Buddhas—it is because their karma and wisdom are respectively superior; the others are born in the remaining manner.
There is no self, only the aggregates, produced by afflictions and karma;
through the continuity of the intermediate state, one enters the womb like a flame.
Just as it is drawn out and gradually increases, this continuity proceeds by means of delusion and karma.
Proceeding further toward other worlds, there is thus a wheel that has no beginning.
Such is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), with its twelve links across the three time periods:
two for each of the prior and subsequent limits, and eight for the middle, based on its full manifestation.
Ignorance is the state of past afflictions; the various past karmas are called formations (*saṃskāra*);
consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the aggregates at the moment of linking rebirth; and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) refers to the period prior to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
From the arising of the faculties such as the eye until the three [feeling, contact, and thirst] precede the six sense bases is the stage of name-and-form.
The differentiation of the causes of the three feelings, not yet fully understood, is called contact (*sparśa*).
Feeling (*vedanā*) occurs prior to sensual craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Greed for the necessities of life and sensual craving, which involve the pervasive pursuit of various objects in order to obtain them, is called grasping (*upādāna*).
Some say that what truly constructs [existence] is the karma that draws forth the fruit of future existence;
the "birth" of future existence is called "becoming," which leads to old age and death when it reaches its state of being experienced.
This tradition permits the explanation in terms of stages; the names of the members are established according to their predominance.
Regarding the past, future, and middle [limits], in order to dispel the delusions of others:
The three afflictions and two karmas, along with seven matters, are also called "fruits.
By abbreviating the fruits and abbreviating the causes, the two [extremes] can be inferred from the middle.
From afflictions arise afflictions and karma; from karma arises the [resultant] entity;
from the entity arise further entities and afflictions—such is the principle of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Herein, the intended meaning is correctly explained: the cause gives rise to the effect once it has already been produced.
It clarifies that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the opposite of what is to be countered (*vipakṣa*),
just as "non-friend" or "untruth" are used [to denote their opposites]. It is designated as a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth because it is not unwise discernment (*dauṣprajña*),
because it is associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), and because it is said to defile discernment (*prajñā*).
The immaterial [sphere] is named the four aggregates; contact arises from the conjunction of three, being sixfold.
Five are associated with resistance; the sixth is accompanied by the designation (adhivacana).
They are luminosity, non-luminosity, and that which is neither; they are untainted, defiled, and the remainder.
Associated with the two—attachment and aversion—and corresponding to the three feelings such as pleasure, six types of feeling arise from these. Five belong to the body and the rest to the mind;
these further become eighteen through the distinctions of the mental applications (*manopavicāra*).
With desire as the object, there are eighteen; with form, twelve; and three from above.
Two have desire as their object, totaling twelve; eight have themselves as their object, and two have the formless.
The final two have desire as their object, totaling six; four have themselves as their object, and one has the formless as its object.
The initial access concentrations of the formless realm take the four form-sphere [dhyānas] as their objects and one of their own;
the four fundamental [dhyānas] and three of the limits take only their own objects.
Eighteen are exclusively with outflows (sāsrava); the rest have been explained or will be explained.
In this context, the afflictions are said to be like seeds and like dragons;
like roots, tree trunks, and stalks; and like rice encased in husks.
Karma is like rice with its husk, and like medicinal herbs and flowers.
All matters that are results of maturation are like cooked food and drink.
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapatti-bhava*) is exclusively defiled by the afflictions of its own level;
the other three existences are likewise [defiled], though in the formless realm there are only three.
Sentient beings subsist through nutriment; In the realm of desire, edible food consists of only three types.
Matter is not [edible food] because it cannot benefit its own sense faculty or liberation.
The three nutriments of contact, volition, and consciousness Are tainted and pervade all three realms.
The mind-made and the seeking-rebirth, The fragrance-eating and the arising from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
The first two benefit this life, As the supported and the supporter;
The latter two pertain to the future existence, As the projecting and the actualizing, respectively.
The severing and reconnecting of the roots of virtue, the departure from passion, falling away, death, and birth—these are held to occur only within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Death and birth occur only with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), and not during meditative absorption or in the two mindless states.
Furthermore, these two [death and birth] are of the nature of the non-defined (*avyākṛta*), as is nirvāṇa.
In the process of gradual death, [the faculties cease] at the feet, the navel, or the heart; finally, the mental consciousness ceases.
Those who do not take rebirth in the lower realms, the heavens, or as humans; those whose vital points (*marmaccheda*) are severed by water and so forth;
those in the categories of the right, the wrong, or the indeterminate; and the noble ones who have committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)—[these are the subjects of this discussion].
Establishing the receptacle world, the wind-circle dwells at the very bottom;
its breadth is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen lakṣas.
Above that is the water-circle, eleven hundred million and twenty thousand [yojanas] deep.
The lower eight hundred thousand *lakṣas* of water, with the remainder congealed into gold,
form this wheel of water and gold. Its diameter is twelve hundred thousand and three thousand four hundred and fifty [yojanas], and its circumference is three times that.
Sumeru stands in the center; next are Yugandhara,
Īṣādhara Mountain, Khadiraka Mountain, Sudarśana, and Aśvakarṇa.
Mount Vinataka and Mount Nimindhara;
outside the great continents and so forth, there is the Cakravāḍa Iron Rim Mountain.
The first seven are composed of gold, while Sumeru is made of the four jewels.
They enter the water to a depth of eighty thousand [yojanas] each; the height of Sumeru is likewise.
The remaining eight mountains decrease by half and half again; their widths are all equal to their heights.
Between these mountains are eight seas; the first seven are called the inner seas.
At its beginning, it is eighty thousand [yojanas] wide; each of its four sides is three times that.
The remaining six are half as wide as the preceding one, in succession.
The eighth is called the Outer [Ocean], measuring three hundred and twenty-two thousand yojanas.
Regarding the characteristics of the great continents: Jambudvīpa in the south is shaped like a chariot;
its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], and its southern side is three and a half.
Pūrvavideha in the east is shaped like a half-moon.
Three sides are like Jambudvīpa; the eastern side is three hundred and fifty [yojanas].
The western continent, Aparagoyānī, is circular and without defect;
its diameter is two thousand five hundred, and its circumference is three times this.
Kuruvara is square, with each side measuring two thousand [yojanas].
There are eight intermediate islands, two for each of the four continents.
To the north of these are nine Black Mountains; within the Snowy Mountains and the Fragrant Mountain lies the Drunken Mountain.
The Lake Anavatapta is fifty yojanas in length and breadth.
Beneath this, at a distance of twenty thousand [yojanas], lies the Avīci hell, equal in depth and breadth.
Above it are the seven *naraka*s, each with eight subsidiary hells (*utsada*), totaling sixteen.
Namely, the Pit of Hot Ashes, the Quagmire of Corpses, the Forest of Sword-Blades, and the River of Boiling Water;
these four increase in size and each occupy one of the four directions. The remaining eight are the cold hells.
The sun and moon are at half the height of Mount Meru, measuring fifty-one and fifty [yojanas] respectively.
At midnight, at sunset, and at midday, the sun rises over the four continents simultaneously.
During the second month of the rainy season, the nights gradually increase for the final nine days;
it is the same during the fourth month of the cold season. When the nights decrease, the days do the opposite.
The *lava* increases day and night as [the sun] travels its northern and southern paths;
because its own shadow covers it when it approaches the sun, the lunar disk appears incomplete.
The Cakravāḍa Mountains have four tiers, each separated from the next by ten thousand [yojanas].
Extending outward sixteen thousand [yojanas], with measurements of eight, four,
and two thousand respectively; the Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādharas, the Sadāmattas,
and the Mahārājikas dwell on the four terraces in order, as do those on the other seven mountains.
The summit of Mount Sumeru is eighty thousand [yojanas] high; there dwell the Trāyastriṃśa gods.
At its four corners are four peaks, where Vajrapāṇi resides.
The central palace is named Sudarśana, measuring ten thousand yojanas in circumference.
Its height is half that of the golden city wall; the ground is adorned with various ornaments and is soft and supple.
In its center stands a preeminent palace, one thousand yojanas in circumference, surrounded by four groves of adornment: Caitraratha, Pāruṣyaka, Miśraka, and Nandana.
The Wondrous Grounds (Sudharmā) occupy the four cardinal directions, each separated by twenty [yojanas].
To the northeast is the Pārijāta tree; to the southwest is the Sudharmā Hall.
Above these are the gods of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu), who dwell in palaces suspended in space.
The six classes of desire-realm beings engage in sexual union through embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing lustfully.
Their lifespans begin at five thousand years and increase up to ten thousand. They possess physical forms that are complete and are clothed.
Three types of desire-realm heavens give rise to desire, while three sets of nine abodes give rise to bliss.
Just as the distance from below is measured, so too is the number of [stages] above;
apart from supernatural power or reliance on another, there is no ascending to see those above.
[There are] the four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, and the heavens of the desire realm.
A thousand worlds of the Brahma realm are called a small chiliocosm;
a thousand times this small chiliocosm is termed a medium chiliocosm;
and a thousand times this is a great trichiliocosm—all of which undergo formation and destruction simultaneously.
The height of the people of Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits or four cubits;
for the people of the eastern, western, and northern continents, it doubles successively in that order.
For the gods of the desire realm, it is one *krośa*, increasing by one-quarter for each successive level.
The *yojana* measurement of the Form Realm heavens: in the first four, it increases by half a half;
above these, it doubles each time; only the Cloudless Heaven (*Anabhraka*) decreases by three.
In the Northern Continent, the lifespan is fixed at one thousand years; in the Western and Eastern continents, it decreases by half and half again.
The lifespan in this continent is indefinite; at the end it is ten years, while at the beginning it is immeasurable.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night in the lowest heaven;
based on this reckoning, their lifespan is five hundred years, with each of the five higher heavens doubling successively.
In the Form Realm, there is no distinction between day and night; the number of kalpas is equal to the measure of the body.
In the Formless Realm, it is twenty thousand kalpas for the first two levels, increasing by two thousand for each subsequent level.
For the gods from the Parīttābha (Limited Light) upward, a full or half kalpa constitutes one kalpa.
In the six hells beginning with Saṃjīva, a day and night is respectively equal to the lifespan of the gods of the Desire Realm; their lifespans are likewise equal to those [gods].
In Pratāpana, it is half an intermediate kalpa; in Avīci, it is a full intermediate kalpa.
The maximum lifespan for animals is one intermediate kalpa; for the Pretas, it is five hundred years by their own month and day.

As for the Ābhāsvara Heaven, its lifespan is like a single *vāha* of sesame seeds, from which one seed is removed every hundred years until they are all exhausted; each subsequent hell increases by twentyfold.
In all realms there is premature death, except for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
The atom (*paramāṇu*), the syllable, and the moment (*kṣaṇa*)—these are the minimum units of form, name, and time respectively.
The *paramāṇu*, the *aṇu*, gold-dust, water-dust, hare-dust, sheep-dust, ox-dust, and mote-dust;
A nit, a louse, a barley grain, and a finger-joint—each subsequent unit increases sevenfold.
Twenty-four finger-joints make one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits constitute the measure of a bow (*dhanus*).
Five hundred *krośas* make eight *yojanas*.
One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute the measure of one tatkṣaṇa;
sixty of these [tatkṣaṇas] are one lava; thirty of these [lavas] are one muhūrta;
thirty of these [muhūrtas] are one day and night; and thirty days and nights are one month.
Twelve months constitute a year; within that, the nights decrease during the middle [half].
When one month and a half of the cold, hot, and rainy seasons have passed, during the remaining fortnight, the wise know that the nights diminish.
One should know that there are four kalpas: namely, the kalpa of destruction, formation, intermediate, and great.
The kalpa of destruction begins from the non-arising of beings in hell and continues until the external receptacle world is completely exhausted.
The kalpa of formation begins from the rising of the wind and continues until the first birth in hell.
An intermediate kalpa begins from an immeasurable lifespan and decreases until life lasts only ten years;
it then undergoes eighteen cycles of increase and decrease, followed by an increase back to eighty thousand years.
Thus, once the world has been formed, it remains for twenty such intermediate kalpas. This is called the period of abiding.
The formation and destruction [of a world], and the period of emptiness after destruction, each lasts for an equal number of *kalpas*.
Eighty intermediate *kalpas* constitute a great *kalpa*, and three incalculable [great] *kalpas* form the duration of a Buddha's career.
When the human lifespan decreases from eighty thousand years down to one hundred, Buddhas appear in the world.
Pratyekabuddhas appear during periods of increase or decrease; those likened to rhinoceros horns do so after a hundred kalpas.
Wheel-turning kings appear when the lifespan is eighty thousand years or more;
with wheels of gold, silver, copper, or iron, they rule over one, two, three, or four continents respectively, following the reverse order, just as with the Pratyekabuddhas and the Buddhas.
They come to him or go to him to submit; though they may prevail in the fray of debate, they do so without harm.
Yet their marks are not perfectly round and luminous; therefore, they are not equal to the Buddha.
At the beginning of the kalpa, they were like the gods of the Form Realm, but later they gradually increased their craving for flavors.
From laziness arises the hoarding of goods, and from that, thieves; to prevent them, fields are hired to be guarded.

As karmic paths increase, lifespan decreases until it reaches ten years, at which point the three calamities appear—of weapons, disease, and famine—in succession, lasting for seven days, seven months, and seven years respectively.

The three calamities are fire, water, and wind; the upper three dhyānas serve as their limits, corresponding respectively to internal calamities and so forth. In the fourth [dhyāna], there is no such movement.
However, those receptacle worlds are not eternal, for they arise and perish simultaneously with the sentient beings therein.
Seven fires and one water; seven cycles of fire and water, followed by wind.
The distinctions of the world arise from karma—namely, volition (*cetanā*) and that which is produced by volition.
Volition is itself mental action (*manas-karma*); that which is produced refers to bodily and vocal actions.
These two types of action— bodily and vocal— are both of the nature of the manifest (*vijñapti*) and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Bodily manifestation is held to be a distinct shape (*saṃsthāna*), not having motion as its essence,
because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) perish in each moment.
Since there can be no such thing as causelessness, the cause of arising must be capable of cessation.
Furthermore, shape is not substantially real, for it would have to be apprehended by two sense faculties.
Since there are no distinct atoms, verbal intimation is admitted to be the sound of speech.
It is taught that there are three types of untainted matter (*anāsravarūpa*), because they increase and are not produced by volition (*akṛta*) and so forth.
Their primary elements (*mahābhūta*), which serve as their basis, are distinct from those upon which informative action (*vijñapti*) depends;
rather, the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of the subsequent moment in the desire realm arises depending on past primary elements.
The impure [non-informative matter] relies on its own level; the pure [non-informative matter] follows the place of its arising.
Non-informative matter is non-appropriated and is also of the nature of outflow and categorized as sentient.
That which is dispersed relies on the nature of outflow, is appropriated, and arises from distinct primary elements.
That which arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is supported by the nourished (*aupacayika*); it is without sensation (*anupātta*) and without distinct great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Manifest action (*vijñapti*) is exclusively of the nature of outflow (*naiṣyandika*); it belongs to the body and is appropriated (*upātta*).
Non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) is the other three [types]; the unwholesome exists only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) pervades both the desire and form realms; informative [action] (*vijñapti*) exists only in the two [realms] where there is sustained thought (*vicāra*).
In the desire realm, there is no obscured informative [action], because it lacks a motivating cause (*samutthāna*).
Ultimate goodness (*paramārtha-kuśala*) is liberation; intrinsic goodness (*svabhāva-kuśala*) consists of shame (*hrī*), dread (*apatrāpya*), and the [wholesome] faculties.
Associated with that, associated therewith, and co-originating material karma and so forth— the opposite of these is called unwholesome.
There are two kinds of co-origination: causal and that of the same moment.
As it should be understood in sequence: they are called "primary" (*pravartaka*) and "concomitant" (*anuvartaka*).
Consciousness abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) is only primary; the five sensory consciousnesses are only concomitant;
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) pertains to both; and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*) or resultant (*vipāka*) is neither.
Regarding the transformation of the nature of wholesome and so forth, the corresponding transformation may each admit three possibilities.
For the Muni, the wholesome is necessarily identical; the neutral may follow or be wholesome.
The non-informative [action] consists of the three types of restraint, as well as non-restraint and that which is neither.
The restraints are the Prātimokṣa, those born of dhyāna, and those born of the Path.
The first restraint is of eight kinds, yet in terms of substantial entity, there are only four.
Because their forms differ and their names vary, each is distinct and not mutually contradictory.
Receiving the abstentions from five, eight, or ten [precepts], and from all that ought to be abstained from,
one is established as a lay devotee (*upāsaka*), one who observes the fast (*upavāsa*), a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), or a monk (*bhikṣu*).
All of these are equally called *śīla*, the sublime conduct, action, and restraint.
Only the initial manifest and unmanifest [karma] are termed "vows" (prātimokṣa) and "paths of action" (karmapatha);

eight [types of practitioners] accomplish the vows of individual liberation (prātimokṣa), while those who have attained dhyāna or who are noble beings (ārya) accomplish the vows born of dhyāna and the paths of action. The latter two types of karma follow the movement of the mind.
Prior to the nine uninterrupted paths, the two [types of restraint] that arise together are called "abandonment.
When combined with correct knowledge and correct mindfulness, they are termed the "restraint of the mental faculty.
Abiding in the non-manifestation (avijñapti) of the Pratimokṣa, as long as it has not been relinquished, one always accomplishes the present [non-manifestation].
After the first moment, they become past; the same applies to non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
One who attains the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*) always possesses it in both the past and the future;
for the Noble One (*ārya*), however, the past is excluded at the beginning. While abiding in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or the Path (*mārga*), one possesses the present.
Abiding in the intermediate state, one possesses the unmanifest [action] (*avijñapti*); at the first moment, one acquires the middle [type], and subsequently, the two [middle and final].

Abiding in restraint or non-restraint, when one gives rise to defiled or pure unmanifest action, at the first moment one acquires the middle [type], and subsequently, the two; this continues until the power of that defilement or purity is exhausted.
The manifest [action] is being accomplished; it is not accomplished in the past or future.
The obscured and unobscured [neutral actions] are accomplished only in the present.
Evil conduct, evil discipline, karma, and the paths of non-restraint—[these are likewise].
One who abides in the intermediate state (*madhyama*) with weak volition (*mṛdu-cetanā*) accomplishes informative action (*vijñapti*), but not non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
A noble one (*ārya*) who has not yet produced informative action accomplishes non-informative action, but not informative action.
One who has attained meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in a stage of concentration accomplishes both; for that noble one, it arises from the attainment of the Path (*mārga*).
The prātimokṣa restraint is acquired through the instruction of another and so forth;
the prātimokṣa restraint lasts for as long as life or for a day and night.
There is no such thing as a day-and-night period for immoral conduct (*duḥśīla*), because it is not received in the same manner as the virtuous vows.
Dwelling in the vicinity [of a teacher], at dawn, one should receive the vows from the master while seated below him;
following the instruction, one should recite the full set of limbs, remaining free from adornments for a day and night.
The limbs of restraint against negligence consist of four, one, and three respectively.
To prevent the commission of natural transgressions, as well as loss of mindfulness and arrogance, the *upavāsa* (fast-day vows) are observed;
others may also possess them. Without having received the Three Refuges, there is no [vow];
by pronouncing oneself a lay devotee (*upāsaka*), the precepts arise, just as it is taught for the bhikṣus and others.
If all were fully endowed with the restraint (*saṃvara*), why speak of "one part" and so forth?
This is said in reference to those who are able to uphold it; [the levels] inferior, middling, and superior follow the mind.
Taking refuge in the Buddha and the Saṅgha refers to the two types of dharmas of the Aśaikṣas.
And with nirvāṇa and analytical cessation—this is said to be the complete taking of the three refuges.
Evil conduct is most censurable; it is easily abandoned and results in non-doing.
One obtains the restraint (saṃvara) according to one's vow; it does not apply to the entire continuum [of the person].
By opening the door to false speech, one transgresses all the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
Among the prohibitions, only the abstention from alcohol is prescribed in order to protect the remaining restraints.
From all [three types of] non-restraint and the two [types of] manifest action, one acquires the restraint of the desire realm.
From the root and at all times, one obtains dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava).
Discipline (saṃvara) arises from all sentient beings; regarding its factors (aṅga) and causes (hetu), it is said to be indeterminate.
Non-discipline (asaṃvara) arises from all [factors], but regarding sentient beings, factors, and causes, it is not so.
The various forms of non-restraint are acquired through action or through formal undertaking;
the remaining types of non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) are acquired through the field, through undertaking, or through intense practice.

One abandons the discipline of individual liberation (*prātimokṣa-saṃvara*) by intentionally relinquishing it, by death, [by losing the faculties, by becoming a hermaphrodite, or by the arising of contrary views].
And when both sexual organs arise together, when the roots of goodness are severed, and at the end of the night;
some say it is by committing a grave offense, while others say it is by the disappearance of the Dharma.
The Kashmiris say that committing these two is like being burdened by debt.
One abandons the wholesome states born of meditative concentration through changing levels or through falling away;
one abandons those of the noble ones through attaining a fruit, refining the faculties, or through falling away.
One abandons the unwholesome discipline through death, or through the arising of both sexual organs upon receiving the discipline.
The abandonment of the intermediate [wholesome] occurs through the force of its reception, through the completion of the task, and through the severance of the life-faculty.
One abandons wholesome states of the desire realm that are not material by means of the severance of the faculties and by being reborn in a higher realm;
one abandons all non-material defiled states by means of the arising of the path of antidote.
Those with immoral discipline exclude the inhabitants of the northern continent, the two types of eunuchs, and those with dual sexual organs;
the discipline of restraint also exists among the gods. Only humans possess all three types of discipline.
Those born in the desire realm heavens and the form realm possess the discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-saṃvara*).

The untainted (*anāsrava*) and those of the formless realm (*ārūpya*), excluding the intermediate dhyāna and the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), are categorized as peaceful, unpeaceful, or neither;
these are termed wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Merit, demerit, and the imperturbable (*āniñjya*): wholesome karma of the desire realm is called merit.
The unwholesome is called non-meritorious.
The wholesome of the upper realms is "immovable," because, with respect to their own level and location, there is no movement regarding the fruit of the karma.
Wholesome [karma] up to the third [dhyāna] is conducive to pleasure; that which is beyond is not so. Wholesome [karma] up to the third [dhyāna] is conducive to pleasure.
All unwholesome [karma] conforms to suffering; the superior wholesome conforms to that which is neither [suffering nor pleasure];
it is said that the remainder also exists in the lower [realms], because they produce maturation from the intermediate [state].
Furthermore, these three types of karma are accepted as such because they do not mature sequentially.
There are five types of feeling in accordance with [its nature]: namely, by way of intrinsic nature, association, object, maturation, and manifestation.
These are further distinguished as being either determinate or indeterminate;
the determinate are the three, such as that which is to be experienced in the present life and so forth.
Some say there are five types of karma; other masters speak of four categories.
Four wholesome karmas may be performed simultaneously, but only three can project a homogeneous existence (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
In all realms, four types of karma are created; however, in the hells, wholesome karma excludes the present.
In the stage of detachment from passion, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) does not create karma for rebirth.
The noble one (*ārya*) does not create karma for rebirth or subsequent existence, nor when falling away from the desire realm or the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
However, in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm, twenty-two kinds of karma can be created.
All are comprised within karma to be experienced in the present life, because their type and homogeneous class are one.
Due to intense affliction or a pure mind, that which is habitually performed,
that which arises toward a field of merit, and the karma of harming one’s parents— such actions are fixed.
Due to the excellence of the field and the intention, as well as karma that definitely brings about maturation,
and karma from a stage of permanent detachment, one will certainly bring about results in the present life.
This applies to the Saṃgha with the Buddha at its head, as well as to those in the attainment of cessation and those free from contention.
Through the paths of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one emerges; karma that causes harm or benefit is experienced immediately.

It is maintained that wholesome karma devoid of vitarka (*avitarka*) produces only mental sensation (*citta-vedanā*), while unwholesome karma produces only bodily sensation (*kāya-vedanā*); such is the distinction between the types of karma that produce sensation.
Mental derangement occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

it arises from the maturation (*vipāka*) of karma, as well as from fear, injury, adverse conditions, and grief. It exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*).
Crooked, corrupt, and turbid karma are said to arise based on guile (*māyā*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and greed (*lobha*).
Based on the distinctions of black, white, and so forth, four types of karma are taught. Evil karma,
wholesome karma of the form and desire realms, that which can exhaust those [former karmas],
and the outflow-free (anāsrava) [karma] should be known, in their respective order, as black-white, both, and neither.
The four dharmakṣāntis and the detachment from desire, together with the eight preceding paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
consist of twelve untainted volitions (*anāsrava-cetanā*) that exhaust only purely black karma.
The ninth path of immediate succession volition during the detachment from each of the four dhyānas [exhausts both black and white karma].
One [type of karma] exhausts the mixed and the purely black; four [types] cause the purely white to be exhausted.

Some say that karma experienced in the hells is black and mixed; others say that karma of the desire realm is black when associated with views to be abandoned by seeing, while the rest of the desire-realm karma is both black and white.
The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the mind—these three are the *mauneya*s (states of sagehood);
they should be known as the three purities and are identical to the three sublime conducts (*sucarita*).
Evil actions of body, speech, and mind are called the three misdeeds (*duścarita*).
As well as greed, hatred, and wrong view—these three unwholesome courses of action;

the opposite of these are the three wholesome courses of action. Among the ten paths of action thus taught, those that are coarse in nature are subsumed within the categories of evil and wholesome conduct, becoming either virtuous or non-virtuous as appropriate.
The six unwholesome [paths] definitely possess non-informative action (avijñapti); those that one performs oneself include sexual misconduct;
the seven wholesome [paths] arise from two types [of volition], while those arising from meditative concentration possess only non-informative action.
In the preparatory stage, informative action (vijñapti) definitely exists, whereas non-informative action may or may not exist.
The subsequent [action] is the opposite of this; it arises from the three roots of application.
Because it arises immediately after that, it is produced by the three roots such as greed and so forth.
Regarding the wholesome, in all three stages, it arises from all three wholesome roots.
Killing, harsh speech, and malice are all ultimately rooted in hatred;
stealing, sexual misconduct, and covetousness are all ultimately rooted in greed;
false view is ultimately rooted in delusion; it is held that the remaining [non-virtuous actions] are rooted in all three.
Sentient beings possess name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which arises based on the aggregates such as name (*nāmakāya*).
Whether they die simultaneously or one dies earlier, there is no separate basis for the faculties (*indriya*) because they are supported by the same [body].
Just as in the case of an army or similar entities acting with a common purpose, all members are considered to have accomplished the act just like the primary agent.
Killing is the intentional taking of life, killing another being without error.
Taking what is not given is to take another’s property by force or stealth for one's own possession.
Sexual misconduct is of four kinds: engaging in sexual acts that are improper.
When one utters words based on a perception different from reality, and the meaning is understood, it is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
That which is apprehended by the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, and mind, as well as the other three [consciousnesses],
is designated, in their respective order, as "seen," "heard," "cognized," and "sensed."
Defiled speech that destroys others is called divisive speech;
unlovely and harsh speech is [abusive speech]; all defiled and miscellaneous frivolous talk is [idle chatter].
Others say that [frivolous talk] differs from the three types of defilement, including flattery, song, and false doctrines.
Covetousness is the desire for the wealth of others; hatred is malice toward sentient beings;
and the view that denies good and evil is called the path of action of wrong view.
Among these, three are exclusively paths, while seven are both actions and paths.
Only wrong view severs the roots of goodness; that which is severed consists of those acquired at birth within the desire realm.
It severs all [roots] by denying cause and effect; they are severed gradually, and both [types of roots] are abandoned.
This occurs among humans in the three continents, for both men and women; it is severed through the path of seeing and is characterized by non-possession (*aprāpti*).
Continuing the roots of goodness occurs through doubt and views; sudden manifestation excludes those who have committed the heinous crimes.
The paths of action and volition operate together: for the unwholesome, from one up to eight;
for the wholesome, generally opening up to ten, though specifically excluding one, eight, and five.
In the unwholesome hells, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and anger are present in both [actual and potential];
greed and wrong view are possessed; in the Northern Continent, the latter three are possessed.
Frivolous speech is both manifest and possessed; for the other ten karmic paths of the desire realm, both are possible.
They are skillful in all places; in the latter three [realms], they are both present and accomplished.
In the formless realms and the heaven of non-perception, the first seven are accomplished only;
in other places, they are both accomplished and present, except for the hells and the northern continent.
All [unwholesome actions] can bring about the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*), and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
This is because they cause others to suffer, terminate life, and destroy one's dignity.
Wholesome bodily and vocal actions arising from greed are difficult to eliminate, for they constitute wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
The craving for the means of livelihood arises from grasping; since this contradicts the Sūtras, it is irrational.
Contaminated karma on the path of abandonment possesses all five fruits;
uncontaminated karma has four, namely, excluding only the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).
The remaining contaminated wholesome and unwholesome [dharmas] also have four [results], excluding the result of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*);
the remaining uncontaminated and neutral [dharmas] have three, excluding those previously excluded.
Regarding wholesome and so forth in relation to wholesome and so forth: the first has four, two, and three [results respectively].
Among these, there are two, three, and four [results]; later, there are two, three, and three results.
For each of the past, there are four; for the present, it is likewise in relation to the future.
For the present, there are two results in the present; for the future, there are three results in the future.
When the cause and effect belong to the same stage (*bhūmi*), there are four fruits; when they belong to different stages, there are two or three.
For those in training (*śaikṣa*), there are three fruits for each of the three causes; for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there is one, three, or two.
For those who are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), there are two, two, and five fruits respectively.
Regarding karma to be abandoned by seeing and so forth, each one has three [results].
In the first [category], there are three, four, and one; in the middle, two, four, and three;
and in the last, one, two, and four. All should be understood according to their respective order.
Defiled karma should not be performed; some say it also violates proper conduct.
Karma that should be performed is the opposite of this; the third category consists of those that are contrary to both.
A single karma draws forth one birth, while multiple karmas are able to bring it to completion.
The two mindless attainments cannot induce other supernormal powers;
nor can the three obstructions, the immediate karmas, the frequently practiced afflictions,
all the evil destinies, the northern continent, or the heaven of non-conception.
The immediate [karmas] exist in the three continents, not among others such as the *śaṇḍha* and so forth;
because they have little gratitude and little shame, other obstructions pertain to all five destinies.
Among these five immediate karmas, four are bodily actions and one is vocal action.
Three [factors] are killing; one is false speech; one is the preparatory effort for taking life.
The schism of the Saṃgha is non-concordance, a formation dissociated from the mind, of an unobscured-neutral nature, and that which is accomplished by the Saṃgha being split.
The schismatic incurs only this offense of false speech;
it ripens for one eon in the Avīci hell, and as the offense increases, so does the suffering.
When a bhikṣu who observes pure conduct causes a schism among the ignorant in another place, [he too incurs this].
When one endures a path different from that of the Teacher, it is called a schism that does not persist beyond a single night.
In Jambudvīpa, nine or more [monks] can bring about a schism of the Wheel;
a schism of the Ritual (Karmasamgha) occurs throughout the three continents with eight or more [monks].
At the beginning and the end, during the period of the twin miracles, before the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa,
and before the boundaries have been established— within these six stages, there is no schism of the Wheel of Dharma.
To abandon or destroy the field of gratitude and virtue constitutes a heinous offense even when one changes one's gender.
The mother refers to her because of that blood; there may be no offense for those who strike by mistake and so forth.
Striking with the intent to kill the Buddha results in shedding his blood. After harming one beyond training (aśaikṣa), there is no [offense].

One who has committed a heinous crime (*ānantarya*) is certain to have undertaken the preparatory action (*prayoga*); there is no attainment of the fruits [of the path] through the abandonment of defilements.
The false speech that causes a schism in the Saṃgha is the greatest among sins;
the volition that brings about rebirth in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is the greatest fruit among worldly virtues.
Defiling one’s mother who is an Arhatī, and killing a Bodhisattva established in the certainty [of enlightenment], [are likewise great transgressions].
Furthermore, for noble ones in training (*śaikṣa*) who disrupt the conditions for the harmony of the Saṃgha or destroy a stūpa—

these are similar to the immediate (*ānantarya*) offenses. They will obstruct the attainment of patience (*kṣānti*) or the stage of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they will act as an obstacle to their karma.

From the cultivation of the karma for the marks of excellence, the Bodhisattva attains the name "one established in meditative concentration," is born into a noble family in a happy realm, and possesses a male body with firm mindfulness.
Being a male of Jambudvīpa facing the Buddha, he is one whose thoughts are accomplished through reflection.
Having spent another hundred kalpas in cultivation, each was adorned with a hundred merits.
Throughout three incalculable eons, he successively made offerings to seventy thousand Buddhas,
and furthermore, in sequence, to five, six, and seven thousand Buddhas.
When the three incalculable eons were complete, he met, in reverse order, the Buddhas Vipasyin,
Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin, and finally Śākyamuni.
Merely through his universal compassion and giving, he felt no anger even when his body was being dismembered.
Having praised Tiṣya Buddha, he then [practiced] unsurpassed bodhi and the six pāramitās; in these four stages,
one, two, and again one, two, he cultivated them to perfection in their respective order.

The three categories of giving, morality, and cultivation each receive the designation of "meritorious action" (*puṇya-kriyā-vastu*) according to their respective natures, with distinctions similar to those of the paths of action (*karmapatha*).
Because it involves relinquishing [possessions], it is called "giving" (*dāna*); that is to say, it is for the purpose of making offerings or for the purpose of benefiting others.
The body, speech, and the motivating impulse—these bring about the fruit of great wealth.
One gives for the benefit of both oneself and others, not for the sake of either alone.
Because of differences in the donor, the object, and the field, there are distinctions in the fruits of giving.
The distinction of the recipient arises from faith and so forth;
by practicing giving with respect and the like, one obtains the fruits of being honored and widely loved, which are timely and difficult to take away.
The distinction of the wealth consists of form and so forth; through it, one obtains a beautiful appearance and a good reputation.
The bodies of those beloved by the multitude are soft and supple, possessing a pleasant touch according to the season;
yet, due to differences in their realms and destinies, there are distinctions in their suffering and their qualities of grace.
Among these, the gift to one who is liberated, and the eighth gift—to a Bodhisattva who is already liberated—is the most supreme.
Parents, the sick, and Dharma teachers, as well as Bodhisattvas in their final birth—
even if they have not yet realized the state of an Arya— the fruit of giving to them is likewise immeasurable.
Furthermore, the field, the fundamental [intention], the preparatory application, the volition, and the mental disposition [all contribute to the magnitude of the result].
Because of these inferior and superior [conditions], karma becomes inferior or superior.
Due to thorough reflection, completion, absence of regret or antidote,
having companions, and having maturation— karma characterized by these is called "accumulated."
The merit derived from offerings to a *caitya* is like that of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the like: it lacks a recipient.
Even in an "unwholesome field," there is a desirable fruit, because the relationship between seed and fruit is never inverted.
Regarding the precepts, there are two types each: those involving the abandonment of natural transgressions and those involving the abandonment of prohibited transgressions.
Not impaired by causes for violating the precepts, it relies on the antidotes and is purified through cessation and so forth.
That which is wholesome in meditative equipoise is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā), because it is supremely able to permeate the mind.
Thus, morality and cultivation are superior in their respective order, leading to rebirth in the heavens and liberation.
The merit of causing others to be born in heaven for an eon and so forth constitutes the measure of a single Brahma-merit (*brahmapuṇya*).
Dharma-giving refers to teaching the sūtras and other texts with unadulterated eloquence according to reality.
There are three types: that which accords with merit, that which accords with liberation, and that which accords with the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
The fruits of feeling and love, Nirvāṇa, and the Noble Path are wholesome in their respective order.
Those arising from correct reasoning, along with the three types of action and their motivating factors,
are respectively the natures of writing, seals, calculation, and literature.
The wholesome and untainted are called "sublime"; the defiled, the blameworthy, the obscured, and the inferior are [otherwise].
Wholesome conditioned phenomena are to be cultivated;
liberation is called "unsurpassed."
The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the root of all existence; they are differentiated into six:
namely, attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
Through the subdivision of attachment, there are seven: attachment to existence pertains to the two upper realms.
Because they operate within the internal door, they serve to exclude the notion of liberation.

Six are distinct from the ten views; these distinctions consist of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Due to differences in the six aspects, the classes, and the realms, there are ninety-eight [defilements].
Those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and so forth in the desire realm number seventeen, seven, seven, and four respectively.
This is because they possess, in order, three, two, two, and one [of the views], as well as view, doubt, and ignorance.
In the form and formless realms, hatred is excluded; the rest are explained as being the same as in the desire realm.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) destroyed by patience are abandoned through insight alone at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
the others are abandoned through both insight and cultivation, while those destroyed by knowledge are abandoned through cultivation alone.
The self and what belongs to the self, annihilationism and eternalism, Denial of existence, regarding the inferior as superior,
and falsely claiming what is not the cause or path to be so— these are the essential natures of the five views.
To falsely cling to Maheśvara and others, who are not the cause, as being the cause;
