Arising from the views of permanence and self, they are therefore abandoned only through the vision of suffering.
The intrinsic nature of the four perversions consists of three views;
because they involve perversion, exaggeration, and augmentation, perception and consciousness follow the power of those views.
The seven types of pride and the nine [types of affliction] arise from the three [roots]; all are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
Like the fetters of killing and so forth, there are those abandoned through cultivation that do not manifest in the Noble Ones.
The sub-types of pride, such as the pride of "I am," and the unwholesome among the [ten] unwholesome courses of action, [are likewise].
The noble ones do not give rise [to these], because they are increased by views and doubt.
Those abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin— namely, the various views associated with doubt,
as well as non-associated ignorance— are pervasive within their own realm and stage.
Among these, excluding two views, the remaining nine are able to take the higher realms as their object;
excluding acquisition (*prāpti*), the remaining concomitants (*anuvartin*) are likewise subsumed under the universal [defilements].
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, which are associated with false view and doubt, [are also universal].
Including the unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*), six [of these] can take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Among those, that which takes cessation (*nirodha*) as its object takes only the cessation of its own stage as its object;
that which takes the path (*mārga*) as its object pertains to six or nine stages, because they serve as mutual remedies for one another.
Greed, hatred, pride, and the two types of grasping do not have uncontaminated objects as their conditions;
they should be abandoned because their objects are not hostile, being of the nature of tranquility, purity, and excellence.
As long as universal latent dispositions have not been severed, they persist toward everything within their own level.
They do not increase universally within their own category, because they increase only with respect to their objects.
They are not without outflows, nor do they take higher levels as objects, because they lack inclusion and involve contradiction.
They increase in accordance with their associated dharmas, because they increase through association.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the two upper realms, as well as the view of self-identity and the view of extremes in the desire realm, along with their associated delusion, are neutral (*avyākṛta*); all others are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The roots of the unwholesome in the desire realm are greed, hatred, and unwholesome delusion.
There are three roots of the indeterminate: indeterminate craving, delusion, and wisdom.
It is not others, because the two [pride and views] are characterized by loftiness. The masters of the West establish four kinds:
craving, views, pride, and delusion; for all three meditative absorptions are accompanied by delusion.
One should respond with categorical distinction, counter-interrogation, or by setting aside the question—
such as regarding death and birth, superiority, or whether the self and the aggregates are one or different.
If, within this matter, greed, hatred, and pride have not been abandoned, [one should remain silent].
If past or present [factors] have already arisen, the future mind-faculty is omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
Five [mental factors] that are subject to arising are omnipresent within their own time; even those not subject to arising are omnipresent.
The remaining [factors] of the past and future are omnipresent; those of the present bind when they are currently taking an object.

The existence of the three time periods is established by their being taught, by the existence of objects and results in two [periods], and by the teaching that the three time periods exist; thus, the Sarvāstivādins are so named.
Within this, there are four types of difference: difference by way of category, state, phase, and relative dependence.
The third [position], which establishes the time periods (*adhvan*) by means of activity (*kāritra*), is the most excellent.
What is the obstacle? What is activity?
If there were no distinction [between the periods], the time periods would be destroyed. Who has not yet arisen? Who has ceased? This nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is exceedingly profound.
When [a defilement] has already been abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*),
the remaining universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) and those of previous categories that have already been abandoned still bind it, provided they take this as their object.
This applies to those abandoned through the vision of suffering and origin (*samudaya-darśana*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), if they are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The three [realms] of one's own sphere and one [realm] of the formless are the objects of untainted consciousness;
the forms of one's own sphere and the lower spheres are each the objects of three [types of] consciousness; the upper [sphere] is the object of one pure consciousness.
The formless [realms] pervade all three spheres, each being the object of three [types of] pure consciousness.
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path all increase the objects of their own respective consciousnesses.
Within the three realms, the last three types of pure consciousness are the objects [of the path].
There are two kinds of minds accompanied by latent dispositions (*anuśaya*): namely, those that are defiled and those that are undefiled.
Defiled minds pertain to both [types of objects]; non-defiled [minds] are restricted to those with which they increase.

Ignorance, doubt, wrong view, views of a self, extreme views, adherence to precepts and rituals, and the views of grasping, greed, pride, and hatred arise in succession, each subsequent one being induced by the preceding.
Because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not been abandoned, and because the corresponding objects appear, and improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) arises,
it is said that the afflictions possess all their causes and conditions. The desire-afflictions (*kāma-kleśa*),
together with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), excluding ignorance (*moha*), are called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
The outflows (*āsrava*) of the two upper realms consist solely of afflictions (*kleśa*), excluding ignorance (*moha*).
Because they are equally indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), internal in nature, and belong to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*), they are combined into one.
Ignorance is the root of all existence; therefore, it is established separately as a distinct outflow.
The floods (ogha) and yokes (yoga) are likewise; they are established separately because views are particularly sharp.
Because views do not conform to abiding, they are not established as independent outflows (āsrava).
The yokes of desire and existence, together with delusion, have views divided into two and named "grasping" (upādāna).
Ignorance is not established separately because it is not a grasper;
its subtle dual increase, its following after, and its binding, its abiding,
flowing, drifting, conjoining, and grasping— these are the meanings of the "latent tendencies" (anuśaya) and so forth.
Due to distinctions such as fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are further said to be of five kinds.
The nine [fetters] consist of the objects of grasping (*upādāna*) and so forth;
the two fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and grasping (*parāmarśa*) are established separately because these two are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*) and arise independently (*svatantra*).
Among the *paryavasthānas*, only envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) are established as two separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).
This is because they frequently occur as a pair, because they are the causes of low birth and poverty,
because they manifest as pervasive secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and because they disturb both groups [of practitioners].
Furthermore, there are five fetters that bind one to the lower realms: by two, one does not transcend the desire realm;
by three, one returns to the lower states. Because they encompass the gates and the faculties, there are three.
Alternatively, they consist of: lack of desire for departure, delusion regarding the path, and doubt regarding the path.
Because they obstruct the approach to liberation, only the abandonment of three is taught.
There are likewise five higher fetters: the two types of craving for the form and formless realms, restlessness, pride, and ignorance;
because they prevent one from transcending the higher [realms].
The three bonds are [defined] by the three feelings; the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have already been explained previously.
The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are the remaining defiled mental factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

There are eight entanglements (*paryavasthāna*): shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), [restlessness], and [doubt].
Restlessness and lethargy, or the ten [factors] when adding anger and concealment—
shamelessness, stinginess, and restlessness— all arise from greed.
Shamelessness, sleep, and lethargy arise from ignorance.
Envy and anger arise from hatred; regret arises from doubt; concealment and contention arise from them as well.
The six afflictions and stains—harmfulness, resentment, guile, deceit, and arrogance—arise [from the primary afflictions];
among these, deceit and arrogance arise from greed.
Malice and resentment arise from hatred; vexation arises from the grasping of views; and flattery arises from various views.
The envelopments of shamelessness, lack of dread, and torpor, as well as lethargy and restlessness, are abandoned through both seeing and cultivation.
The remaining [envelopments] and the defilements of the afflictions are abandoned only through cultivation, because they function independently.
The three [types of] desire are [associated with] two [realms], while the remaining unwholesome [states] are [associated with] the rest; in the higher realms, all are neutral.
Deceit and guile exist in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna; the three [types of] desire exist in the three realms, while the rest exist in the Desire Realm.
Pride and torpor abandoned through insight are independent secondary afflictions.
All [of these] arise solely on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*); the others may depend on all six consciousnesses.
The various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are associated with joy and pleasure when they are greed;
hatred is associated with sorrow and pain; delusion is universal; and false view is associated with both sorrow and joy.
Doubt and mental distress are associated with the remaining five [mental factors], while all are associated with equanimity.
In the higher stages, they are each associated as appropriate with the various feelings of their own respective consciousnesses.
Among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), envy, regret, anger, and vexation—
Harmfulness and resentment arise together with sorrow; stinginess is associated with joy and feeling.
Flattery, deceit, torpor, and concealment arise universally with both sorrow and joy.
Arrogance is associated with joy, pleasure, and equanimity; the remaining four are universally associated.
The five hindrances exist only in the desire realm; because their objects and remedies are the same, although there are two [types of craving], they are established as a single hindrance.
They are only five because they obstruct the aggregates, because they universally know their objects, and because they sever those that take them as objects.
Because their objects are severed, and because the antidote arises, they are abandoned.
There are four kinds of antidotes— namely, abandonment, maintenance, distancing, and aversion—
one should know that through these, the various afflictions can be brought to cessation based on their objects.
Remoteness is of four kinds: by way of characteristic, antidote, location, and time;
as in the case of the primary elements, morality, different locations, and the two periods of time.
Defilements are not severed twice, yet disconnection may be acquired repeatedly.

That is to say: during the six occasions of attaining the fruits through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), there are nine types of thorough knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*). Among these, one is attained at the abandonment of the first two categories of afflictions in the desire realm;
two are attained at the abandonment of each of the remaining two categories, totaling three; and the same applies to the three categories of the higher realms.
The remaining five [fetters] are the lower-tier fetters; the three [fetters] are severed entirely in the form realm.
Among these, six are the fruits of patience (kṣānti), and the remaining three are the fruits of knowledge (jñāna).
In the preliminary stage (anāgamya), all are fruits; in the fundamental [dhyānas], there are either five or eight.
The fruit of the Peak of Formlessness is one; the same applies to the three fundamental [dhyānas].
There are two worldly fruits and nine noble fruits. Dharma-knowledge has three, and subsequent knowledge has two.
The fruits of the category of dharma-knowledge are six; the fruits of the category of subsequent knowledge are five.

Because one attains the acquisition of the abandonment of outflows (*anāsrava-prahāṇa-lābha*), and because of the deficiency of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the extinction of the two causes, and the transcendence of realms, nine universal knowledges (*parijñā*) are established.
They do not exist while abiding in the stage of seeing the truths (*darśana-mārga*); otherwise, one may possess from one up to five.
In the path of cultivation, one attains six, one, or two; in the stage of no-more-learning, one attains only one.
Because of transcending realms and attaining fruits, the two locations (the path of seeing and the path of cultivation) involve the accumulation of universal knowledges (*parijñā*);
one abandons one, two, five, or six, and the acquisition is likewise, except for the abandonment of five.
It has already been explained that the abandonment of afflictions occurs through the paths of seeing and cultivation;
the path of seeing is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), while the path of cultivation pertains to both types.
The four truths have already been named: namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Their own nature is likewise so, following the sequence of clear realization.
Suffering arises from the conjunction of the three types of suffering;
as appropriate, this applies to all things—whether agreeable, disagreeable, or other contaminated conditioned phenomena.
That which ceases when its cognition is broken, And likewise that which remains when analyzed by wisdom— Such as a jar or water, is conventional; Anything other than this is called the ultimate.
One who is about to enter the path of seeing the truths Should abide in ethical discipline and practice with diligence.
Those produced by hearing, reflection, and cultivation—namely, the objects consisting of names, words, and meanings—are characterized by physical and mental seclusion.
To be free from lack and great desire means that one does not seek much for what has already been obtained or what has not yet been obtained; such seeking is absent in the noble ones.
The three [types of contentment] counteract the three discordant factors; they are untainted and have non-attachment as their nature.
The four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) are likewise; the first three consist solely of contentment.
Three concern the requisites of life, and the last concerns one's livelihood; they are established to counteract the arising of the four types of craving.

Because of the desire for "mine," "self," and "my affairs," one enters the two essential gates of cultivation— impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*)— to temporarily suppress and permanently eliminate them;
those in whom craving and discursive thought predominate should practice these respectively.
To universally counteract the four types of craving, one first contemplates the skeletal chain;
expanding the visualization as far as the ocean and then contracting it again is called the stage of a beginner.
Extending from the feet up to half the head is called the stage of one who has already matured their practice.
Fixing the mind between the eyebrows is called the stage of transcending mental application (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).
Its nature is non-attachment; it consists of ten stages; it takes beings of the desire and form realms as its object; it arises from the contemplation of the foul (*aśubhā*);
it takes its own world as its object; it is contaminated (*sāsrava*); and it is acquired through both types of attainment.
Mindfulness of breathing has wisdom as its nature and belongs to five stages; it takes wind as its object, relies on a body in the desire realm, and is attained in two ways.
It is real and does not exist externally. There are six types, namely counting and so forth.
Inhalation and exhalation follow the body and proceed according to two distinctions.
The mental factors are not grasped; they are outflows and do not take lower levels as objects.

Having already cultivated and perfected śamatha, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness for the sake of vipaśyanā, observing body, sensation, mind, and phenomena by way of their specific and general characteristics.
The wisdoms of hearing and so forth are intrinsic; the others are mixed and have objects of focus.
They are taught in sequence according to their arising, and there are only four because they counteract the perversions.
These abide in the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), observing the four objects of focus collectively.
One cultivates the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
From this, the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) arises, wherein one contemplates the Four Noble Truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects.
Subsequently, the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan) arises in the same manner.
These two roots of goodness both consist of the first [dharma] followed by the four;
next, patience consists only of the mindfulness of dharmas. The lower and middle grades are the same as the summit (*mūrdhan*).
The upper grade contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm; it is a single practice and lasts for a single moment.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma is likewise; all are wisdom, excluding acquisition.
These are the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); all four are produced by cultivation (*bhāvanā-maya*).
They exist in six stages, or seven for two [of them]; they rely on the body of the desire realm and consist of nine [minds].
Three and the male obtain two; the fourth female is likewise.
The noble ones relinquish them by losing their stage; ordinary beings do so by death.
The first two are also relinquished through falling away; based on the fundamental [attainment], one must necessarily see the truths.
What is abandoned has not been previously attained; the two types of abandonment are of the nature of non-possession (*aprāpti*).
The stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) necessarily leads to Nirvāṇa; the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*) never severs the roots of goodness.
The stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) does not lead to rebirth in the evil destinies; the first [dharma] enters the state beyond birth (*niyāma*).
Those of the śrāvaka lineage may transform: two become Buddhas, while three remain as others;
the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha] and the Buddha do not transform, because they attain awakening in a single sitting.
As for the *muktimārga-anuloma* (preparatory factors conducive to liberation), through three rapid lifetimes, one attains liberation.
The three types of karma—those of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—are planted in the three continents of human beings.

Immediately following the "Supreme Mundane Dharma," one takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object and gives rise to the "Dharma-patience" of the untainted dharma. Following this patience, the "Dharma-knowledge" arises.
Next, taking the suffering of the remaining realms as object, there arise the Patience and Knowledge of Suffering;
likewise, taking the Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path as objects, four each are produced.
These sixteen moments of mind are called the "Clear Realization of the Noble Truths."
This [patience] is of three kinds in total: namely, patience regarding the vision of the object and patience regarding the discernment of particulars;
all share the same stage as the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Patience and knowledge follow their respective order as the path of uninterrupted transition and the path of liberation.
The first fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees what was never seen before.
Based on the distinction between dull and sharp faculties, these are named "followers by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) and "followers by dharma" (*dharmānusārin*).
Having abandoned from one up to five categories of afflictions through cultivation, they are candidates for the first fruit (*srota-āpanna-phala-pratipannaka*).
Having abandoned the next three [categories of afflictions], one is headed for the second fruit; having abandoned the eight [categories], one is headed for the third.

Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, one abides in the fruit according to whichever of the three paths they were headed for, being designated as "one resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) or "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta), distinguished further by dullness or sharpness of faculties.
Among the various stages of attaining the fruits [of the path], because the path to a superior fruit has not yet been attained, the superior path has not yet arisen;
thus, one is said to "abide in the fruit" rather than being "heading toward it.
In each stage (*bhūmi*), there are nine faults and virtues, consisting of three each—lower, middle, and upper.
If one has not yet abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation, one who abides in the fruit will undergo at most seven more rebirths.
Having abandoned three or four categories of desire, one is a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner, undergoing three or two more births.
From the abandonment up to the fifth category, one is a candidate for the second fruit; having abandoned six categories, one attains the fruit of once-returner.
Having abandoned seven or eight categories [of afflictions], one who has one birth remaining is called an *ekavīcika*;
this is the third stage of the path (*pratipannaka*). Having abandoned nine categories, one attains the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
Among these, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*) and those who attain it without exertion (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*).

If those who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas) have practiced the mixed meditations (vyavakīrṇabhāvanā), they can go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven by means of leaping, half-leaping, or passing away entirely; others can go to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
There are four types of practitioners regarding the formless realm (ārūpya), and some attain parinirvāṇa while remaining here [in the desire realm].
There are nine destinies within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), namely, three each divided into three;
due to distinctions in karma, afflictions, and faculties, they thus constitute the distinction of three groups of nine.
The seven "noble person" destinies (*satpuruṣagati*) are established, because the "upward-streamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) has no further subdivisions.
Because good and evil deeds are either practiced or not, there is going forth but no returning.
A noble one born in the desire realm does not go to be born in another realm;
such a person, as well as those born in higher realms, neither refine their faculties nor undergo regression.
First, one practices the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna; its accomplishment arises from a single moment of mixing.
This is for the sake of rebirth, present enjoyment, and the prevention of falling away through afflictions.
By practicing five grades of mixed cultivation, there arise the five Pure Abodes.
One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation and is a non-returner is further designated as a "bodily witness" (kāyasākṣin).
Among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the higher realms, from the abandonment of the first grade of the first dhyāna up to the eighth grade of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra),
all such individuals are candidates for arhatship (arhattvaprati-pannaka).
The ninth path of immediate succession is called the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*);
together with the attainment of exhaustion, it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), whereby one becomes an adept (*aśaikṣa*) and attains the fruit of arhatship.
Defilements of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are abandoned through the untainted [path], while the remainder are abandoned through both [the untainted and the tainted paths].
The two noble paths and the eight stages of cultivation each possess two types of acquisition of disjunction (*visamyoga-prāpti*).
The untainted path of the *anāgamya* stage can bring about disjunction from all stages;
the remaining eight [untainted paths] bring about disjunction from their own and higher stages; the tainted paths bring about disjunction from the immediately lower stage.

The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) sever the defilements of the lower levels; the first three [of these] and the final liberation consist of either the fundamental or the preparatory stage. For the higher levels, there is only the fundamental stage.
The worldly path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the lower and upper levels as their objects, respectively.
One performs the three contemplations of coarseness, suffering, and obstacles, as well as those of tranquility, excellence, and detachment.
Following the knowledge of cessation (*kṣayajñāna*) in the immovable [stage], one necessarily gives rise to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
In other cases, it may be the knowledge of cessation or right view; these are all present in the fruit of arhatship.
The path of purification and the nature of a śramaṇa, With their conditioned and unconditioned fruits—these number eighty-nine: The paths of liberation and cessation.
The four fruits are established by five causes: The abandoning of what was previously attained and the acquisition of a superior path.
Upon the attainment of abandonment through the path of accumulation, one acquires eight knowledges and simultaneously cultivates the sixteen aspects.
Because that which is abandoned by the mundane path is mixed with that attained by the noble [supramundane] path,
and because it is sustained by untainted acquisition (*anāsrava-prāpti*), it is also called a fruit of śramaṇaship.
That which is called the nature of a śramaṇa is also named a brāhmaṇa,
and is also called the Brahma-wheel, because it is turned by the True Brahmā.
Within this, only the Path of Seeing is designated as the Wheel of Dharma.
Because they are swift and so forth, resembling a wheel, or because they possess spokes and other such parts.

Three rely on the desire realm; the latter three do not, because in the higher realms there is no path of seeing, no hearing [of the Dharma], and no perception of the lower realms, due to the absence of revulsion and because of the sūtras.
There are six types of arhats, ranging from those subject to regression to the immovable.
The first five arise from the stage of faith-understanding and are collectively termed "those liberated by occasion.
The latter is "liberated not by occasion," arising from the stage of vision-attainment.
Some possess this from their original lineage; some acquire it later through the refinement of faculties (*indriya*).
Four [types of persons] may fall away from their lineage; five may fall away from the fruit, but not from the former [lineage].
Learners (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) likewise have six [cases]; the refinement of faculties does not occur during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
One should know that there are three types of falling away: from what has been attained, from what has not yet been attained, and from enjoyment.
For a Buddha, there is only the last; for those of sharp faculties, the middle and the last; for those of dull faculties, all three.
One who falls away from any fruit will certainly attain it again before death.
What is not done by one abiding in the fruit is not done because of increased shame.
In the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Because they have long been practiced, in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) there is only one [such path]. These untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties rely on three types of persons.
The one beyond training relies on nine stages; the one in training relies on only six.
This is because they have abandoned the path of the fruit and the path of superior fruits, retaining only the path of the fruit itself.
Regarding the seven types of śrāvakas and the two Buddhas, their distinctions arise from the nine faculties.
Through the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the faculties (*indriya*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and liberation (*vimukti*), seven [types] are established.
As for the distinctions among these entities, there are only six, because each of the three paths has two types.
All [of these] obtain the attainment of cessation; those others are called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*).
The learner (śaikṣa) is called "perfected" by virtue of three factors: faculties, fruits, and meditative absorptions (samāpatti);
the non-learner (aśaikṣa) receives the name "perfected" through two factors alone: faculties and meditative absorptions.
One should know that all paths, when briefly stated, are of only four types.
That is to say: the path of preparation, the uninterrupted path, the path of liberation, and the path of excellence.
There are four types of paths of practice: those based on the fundamental dhyānas are pleasant, while those based on the remaining stages are painful;
they are slow or swift according to whether the faculties are dull or sharp.
The factors of enlightenment are thirty-seven, namely the four foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
"Enlightenment" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising; because they accord with this, they are called "factors.
In terms of actual entities, there are only ten: namely, wisdom, diligence, concentration, and faith.
Mindfulness, joy, equanimity, and pliancy, as well as ethical discipline and investigation, constitute their essence.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power are designated as wisdom, diligence, and concentration, respectively, according to their predominant factor; in reality, they are all wholesome states of application.
In the stages of the beginner, the aids to penetration, and the paths of cultivation and seeing,
one should know that the seven categories— beginning with the foundations of mindfulness— increase in sequence.
The seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold path are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).
The five faculties and powers of the third and fourth [dhyānas] both pertain to two kinds.
All [factors] of the first dhyāna are present; in the *anāgamya* stage, the faculty of joy (*saumanasya*) is excluded.
In the second dhyāna, applied thought (*vitarka*) is excluded; in the third and fourth [dhyānas], both [applied and sustained thought] are excluded.
In the first three formless stages, the two preceding types [of pure faith] are excluded from the precepts;
in the desire realm and the Peak of Existence, the factors of enlightenment and the path members are excluded.
There are four kinds of verified purity (avetyaprasāda), namely: in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and the precepts.
Upon seeing the three [truths], one attains the Dharma-precept; upon seeing the Path, one also attains the Buddha- and Sangha-precepts.
"Dharma" refers here to the entirety of the three truths and the paths of the Bodhisattva and Pratyekabuddha.
These two—faith and precept—are their essential nature; all four are exclusively untainted (anāsrava).
Because those in training still possess residual fetters, they lack the factor of the knowledge of right liberation.
Liberation is both conditioned and unconditioned; the latter refers to the cessation of the supreme delusion.
The conditioned factors of one beyond training are precisely the two aggregates of liberation.
Right knowledge is as explained regarding awakening; it refers to the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising.
When the mind of one beyond training arises, it is correctly liberated from its obstacles.
The path exists only at the moment of ceasing, and it is capable of severing those obstacles.
The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) speaks of three realms: the realm of detachment is solely the detachment from craving;
the realm of abandonment is the abandonment of the remaining fetters; the realm of cessation is the cessation of those phenomena.
Wisdom that takes suffering and its origin as its object brings about weariness; wisdom that takes the four truths as its object brings about detachment and the power of abandonment.
Relative to one another, they are mutually broad or narrow; thus, four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
Noble wisdom (*āryaprajñā*) and receptivity (*kṣānti*) are not knowledge (*jñāna*); the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not vision (*dṛṣṭi*).
The remaining two types of outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravaprajñā*) are both knowledge; six [of these] have the nature of vision.
Wisdom is, in brief, of two kinds: distinguished as contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
That which is contaminated is called conventional (*saṃvṛti*); that which is uncontaminated is named dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Conventional wisdom takes all things as its object; dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge [take their respective objects].
Respectively, those directed toward the desire realm and the higher realms take the truths of suffering and so forth as their objects.
Because of the distinction in their objects, the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are established under the four names of suffering and so forth.
Both are common to the knowledges of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); however, the former [subsequent knowledge] applies only to the categories of suffering and origin.
The knowledge of others' minds consists of the Dharma-knowledge, the Subsequent-knowledge, the Path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge;
it does not know [the minds of others] regarding superior stages, faculties, or states, nor those of the past or future.
The Dharma-knowledge and Subsequent-knowledge do not know one another; as for the Śrāvakas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Buddhas:
In this order, one knows and sees the path; in two or three moments, one knows all.

Regarding the four noble truths, through the cognitions "I have known" and so forth, and "there is no more to be known" and so forth, there arise respectively the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
Based on their intrinsic nature, their antidotes, their aspects, their objects,
their preparatory application, their accomplishment, and the perfection of their causes, ten knowledges are established.
The knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and the path, within the stage of the path of cultivation, [are distinguished].
Simultaneously, they treat the upper realms and cultivate abandonment; the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) cannot treat the desire realm.
Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge possess sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) each;
conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) possesses these and others, with four types of knowledge for each of the Four Truths.
The knowledge of others' minds that is untainted (anāsrava) consists of only four [knowledges], namely those taking the Path as their object;
when tainted (sāsrava), it takes specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) as its object. Both take only a single thing as their object.
The knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising consist of fourteen [knowledges], excluding emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-self (anātman).
Purity does not exceed sixteen [aspects], for other [teachers] state that there are more;
the aspects are actually sixteen. Their essence is exclusively wisdom (*prajñā*);
they are able to act upon objects, and their objects of action are all existent phenomena.
The mundane [knowledges] are three, nine, and wholesome; those based on the stages are all mundane.
The knowledge of others' minds is only fourfold; the dharma-knowledge is sixfold, and the remaining seven are ninefold.
Regarding the bodies upon which they arise: the knowledge of others' minds relies on the desire and form realms.
The knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) relies solely on the desire realm; the remaining eight pertain to all three realms.
Regarding the inclusion of these knowledges within the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna): the knowledge of cessation is included in the last one alone;
the knowledge of others' minds is included in the final three; and the remaining eight knowledges pertain to all four.
The various knowledges take one another as their objects: Dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge each have nine objects;
Knowledge of suffering and knowledge of origin each have two; All four have ten, while knowledge of cessation has none.
In total, there are ten objects, namely: those of the three realms and the untainted.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) each have two; the conventional has ten objects, while the [knowledge of] dharmas has five.
The [knowledge of] categories has seven, and that of suffering and origin has six. The knowledge of cessation has one object, and that of the path has two.
The knowledge of others' minds has three objects; the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising each have nine.
Conventional knowledge, excluding its own category, takes all phenomena as its collective object;
it has the aspect of "non-self" and is produced solely by hearing and reflection.
For ordinary beings and noble ones at the first moment of the path of seeing, it is definitely established as one.
In the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), three knowledges (*jñāna*) are established; in the latter four, one is added at each stage.
In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), seven are definitely established; for those free from desire, the knowledge of others' minds is added.
For those in the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the dull-witted establish nine, while those of sharp faculties establish ten.
When the patiences and knowledges arise in the path of seeing, those very same [patiences and knowledges] are cultivated in the future;
the three types of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) are cultivated concurrently, as is the conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*).
It does not arise from its own stage or a lower stage; following the four [knowledges] regarding suffering and origin, it arises after the knowledge of cessation.
Taking the aspects and objects of the Truths as its own, it is obtained solely through application.
At the first moment of the Path of Cultivation, one cultivates six or seven knowledges;
during the uninterrupted paths that abandon the eight stages, as well as on the remaining paths for those still possessing desire.
In the eight liberations of the Peak of Existence, one cultivates seven knowledges in each;
in the subsequent paths of uninterrupted transition, one cultivates six and eight respectively.
In the first moment of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one cultivates nine or ten.
Due to the distinction between dull and sharp faculties, the path of superior progress is likewise.
In the uninterrupted paths of the refinement of faculties, those in training have six; those beyond training have seven.
For others in training, there are six, seven, or eight; for those beyond training, there are eight, nine, or all [nine].
In the uninterrupted path of the mixed cultivation of the supernormal powers, the learner (śaikṣa) cultivates seven, while the adept (aśaikṣa) cultivates eight or nine;
in other paths, the learner cultivates eight, while the adept cultivates nine or all [nine].
When the noble ones give rise to other qualities, as well as in all the stages of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), [the same principles apply].
The extent of the wisdom cultivated should all be considered according to reason.
When attaining a certain path, one cultivates the contaminated [wisdom] of that stage;
when arising from detachment, one cultivates the uncontaminated [wisdom] of that stage and its lower stages.
Only at the initial moment of exhaustion does one cultivate all [virtues] throughout the nine stages;
as for the outflowing virtues (*sāsrava-guṇa*), when born in a higher stage, one does not cultivate those of lower stages, nor does one cultivate what has already been attained.
One establishes the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*) based upon wholesome conditioned phenomena (*kuśala-saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Based on all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*), one establishes the cultivation of remedies (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*) and the cultivation of elimination (*vinirdhāvanabhāvanā*).
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*)—namely, the ten powers (*bala*) of the Buddha and so forth—the powers consist of ten:
the ten [powers] regarding the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), with the eight [kinds of] karma excluding [the paths of] cessation and the path.
The faculties, roots, liberations, and elements are nine; the knowledge of the path leading everywhere is nine or ten.
The conventional knowledge of past lives and of death and rebirth consists of six or ten knowledges.
The knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of death and rebirth rely on the dhyānas; the remaining supernormal powers rely on all [four] dhyānas.
The body of a Jambūdvīpa male Buddha is unimpeded with respect to its objects;
it possesses the strength of Nārāyaṇa, or rather, each and every joint does so.
This strength increases through seven stages, beginning with that of an elephant and so forth; its essential nature is the sense-base of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
The four fearlessnesses correspond, in order, to the first, the twelfth, and the seventh powers;
the three foundations of mindfulness consist of mindfulness and wisdom, taking as their objects conditions that are favorable, unfavorable, or both.
Great compassion consists solely of conventional knowledge; its provisions, aspects, and objects are as previously described.
Because they are equal and supreme, compassion differs [from them] due to eight causes;
yet, by virtue of their accumulations, dharma-body, and benefit for others, Buddhas are similar.
Regarding lifespan, lineage, measure, and so forth, there are differences among the Buddhas.
Furthermore, there are other qualities of the Buddha that are shared with other noble ones and ordinary beings, namely:
the absence of strife (*araṇā*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and other such virtues.
The absence of strife is conventional knowledge; it belongs to the final dhyāna and is unshakable.
The three continents are its object; it has not yet arisen. It takes as its object the active afflictions of the desire realm.
The knowledge resulting from prayer can take all things as its object. The rest is as explained regarding the absence of conflict (*araṇā*).
There are four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), namely: those of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence.
The analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) regarding names, meanings, speech, and paths have non-retrogressive wisdom as their nature;
those concerning phenomena (dharma) and language (nirukti) consist only of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna). They rely on five and two stages respectively;
the knowledge of meanings consists of sixteen aspects, while the others consist of nine, all of which rely upon all stages.
When attained, they must necessarily possess four [factors]; the rest is as explained in the section on the "Non-contentious" (*araṇā*).
The six are attained based on the "limit" (*prāntakoṭika*); the limit refers to the six [meditative attainments] following the final concentration (*dhyāna*).

They are universal, conformable, and reach the ultimate; for the Buddha, they are attained through cultivation (*prayoga*), whereas for others, they are attained through preparatory effort (*prayoga-labdha*).

The six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) consist of the power of the miraculous, the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows. They are subsumed under the wisdom of the path of liberation.
Four are conventional; the knowledge of others' minds is fivefold; the power of the exhaustion of outflows is like the [ten] powers.
Based on the four dhyānas, they take their own level and lower levels as objects.
For Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, these extend to two thousand, three thousand, and incalculable world-systems respectively.
Those not previously cultivated are attained through preparatory effort; those previously cultivated are attained through the abandonment of defilements.
The first three applications of mindfulness consist of the body; the knowledge of others' minds consists of three; the remaining four consist of all four.
The divine eye and ear are neutral (*avyākṛta*); the other four supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
The fifth, second, and sixth are "clear knowledges" (*vidyā*), because they counteract ignorance regarding the three time periods.
The latter two are real; the first two are conventional designations. Among those who study, some are obscured and not luminous.
The first, fourth, and sixth are guides; among these, the guide of instruction is supreme.
Concentration is accomplished through supernormal powers, for it draws forth the fruits of benefit and happiness.
The essence of the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); its objects are twofold: movement and transformation. Movement is threefold:
by will, by mental power, and by the Buddha. It consists of bodily transport and resolute conviction.
Transformation is twofold: pertaining to the desire realm and the form realm; it has the nature of four or two external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
Each of these is of two kinds, namely: resembling one's own body or another's body.

The transformative minds are fourteen; as results of meditative concentration, they range from two to five, obtained according to the concentration upon which they rely. From the pure [mind], two arise spontaneously.
The emanated body arises from its own level; speech may arise from its own level or a lower one.
The emanated body and its master always possess speech together, yet neither is necessarily a Buddha.
Having first established a vow to retain the body, one subsequently gives rise to other minds and speech.
Some maintain that death leaves behind a solid body; others say there is no such sense of "leaving behind.
At first, many minds produce a single transformation; once perfected, this is the opposite.
That which is acquired through cultivation is subsumed under the neutral (avyākṛta); the rest are obtained as belonging to all three natures.
The divine eye and ear are faculties; they consist of pure matter (*rūpa*) belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*).
They are always of the same class (*sabhāga*) and unimpaired, perceiving what is obstructed, subtle, distant, and so forth.

The supernormal power of the base (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*) is fivefold: produced by cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), birth (*upapatti-ja*), incantations (*mantra-ja*), medicinal herbs (*auṣadha-ja*), and the accomplishment of karma (*karmaja*).
The knowledge of others' minds arises from cultivation, birth, or incantations; it is further accomplished through the interpretation of signs.
The three types of knowledge arise from cultivation, birth, or karma. With the exception of cultivated knowledge, all are of the three natures.
Humans alone possess the knowledge of non-arising; those in hell can first know [others' minds] at the moment of birth.
The four dhyānas each have two [types]; those born therein have already been explained.
Concentration (samādhi) is defined as being wholesome and one-pointed; together with its attendants, it has the nature of the five aggregates.
The first possesses vicāra, prīti, and sukha; the subsequent ones gradually abandon the preceding factors.

The formless [attainments] are likewise; the four aggregates, free from the lower stages, together with the three preparatory stages of the upper realms, are collectively termed "removal of the perception of form.
"Formless" means the absence of form; subsequent forms arise from the mind.
The three beginning with Infinite Space are named according to their preparatory application (*prayoga*);
Non-perception and Non-non-perception are named because they are dull and inferior.
These are the eight fundamental attainments (*mauladhyāna*); of these, the first seven each have three types.
They are called "tasting," "pure," and "untainted"; the latter two consist of both "tasting" and "pure.

"Tasting" refers to that which is associated with craving; "pure" refers to mundane wholesomeness, which is precisely what is relished and clung to; "untainted" refers to that which transcends the world.
The first dhyāna has five factors: vitarka, vicāra, prīti, sukha, and samādhi;
the second has four factors: adhyātmasaṃprasāda, prīti, sukha, and samādhi;
the third possesses five factors: upekṣā, smṛti, prajñā, sukha, and samādhi.
The fourth [dhyāna] has four factors: equanimity, mindfulness, neutral feeling, and concentration.
These actual entities number eleven: the first two [factors] are bliss and pliancy;
inner serenity is the faculty of faith; and joy is the feeling of joy.
The defilements follow in order from the beginning: [the first dhyāna] lacks joy and bliss; [the second] has internal purity;
[the third] has right mindfulness, wisdom, equanimity, and mindfulness; others say it lacks tranquility and equanimity.
The fourth is called "unshakable" because it is free from the eight calamities.
The eighth [dhyāna] consists of vitarka and vicāra; the four [lower dhyānas] include inhalation and exhalation.

From the first, the meditative absorptions arise with the feelings of joy and bliss, and with joy-bliss- equanimity, and joy-equanimity-bliss; in the last, there is only the feeling of equanimity, respectively.
When one is born in the three higher dhyānas, the minds that give rise to the three types of informative [action] are all subsumed under the first dhyāna; they are exclusively non-obscured neutral.
These are acquired entirely through non-possession, while the pure [informative action] arises from the abandonment of defilements.
The untainted [attainment] arises from detachment; the tainted, from birth or retrogression.
The untainted is followed by the wholesome, extending up to the third level above or below.
The pure [attainment] follows in the same manner, additionally giving rise to the tainted of its own level.
From a defiled [attainment], one produces its own pure or defiled [attainment], as well as the pure of the stage immediately below;
at death, from the pure, one produces all [types]; from a defiled, one produces its own or those of the stages below.

There are four kinds of pure concentrations, namely: the part conducive to decline (*hāna-bhāgīya*), [the part conducive to maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya*), the part conducive to distinction (*viśeṣa-bhāgīya*), and the part conducive to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*)].
The stages that accord with abiding, accord with superior progress, and are subsumed under the levels conducive to penetration correspond,
in order, to the afflictions, their own stage and higher stages, and the untainted (anāsrava) states;
when these are viewed in relation to one another, they give rise to two, three, three, and one [results] respectively.
The two types of meditative attainments proceed both in direct and reverse order; they may be practiced with equal intervals, in immediate succession, or by skipping stages.
Success is achieved when one reaches the stage of skipping intervals. These pertain to those of sharp faculties who are non-learners (aśaikṣa) in the three continents.
All meditative attainments depend upon their own level or a lower one, but not upon a higher level, because there would be no purpose in doing so.
Only the noble ones born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) can give rise to [the attainment of cessation] and exhaust the remaining afflictions of the lower realms.
The "tasting" concentration (*āsvādana-samādhi*) takes its own level’s fetters as its object; the pure (*śuddha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) concentrations take all levels as their objects.
The wholesome formless attainments of the fundamental states do not take the contaminated phenomena of lower levels as their objects.
The untainted [attainments] can sever the afflictions, as can the various pure access concentrations (*sāmantaka*).
Among these, the eight access concentrations are equanimous and pure; the first is also noble (*ārya*) or of three types.
The intermediate dhyāna is without vitarka, possesses all three [types of concentration], and consists solely of the feeling of equanimity.
The first [dhyāna] possesses both vitarka and vicāra; the middle [dhyānas] possess only vicāra, while the upper [dhyānas] have neither.
"Emptiness" refers to emptiness and non-self; "signlessness" refers to the four aspects of cessation;
"wishlessness" refers to the remaining ten aspects, which are associated with the aspects of the truths.
This supernormal power is both pure and untainted; as for the untainted, it consists of the three doors of liberation.
It takes the two [aspects] of the non-learner twice, grasping the characteristics of emptiness and impermanence.
Subsequently, it takes the concentration on the signless, regarding analytical cessation as tranquility.
For those with outflows who are not occasional, having abandoned the seven higher access concentrations,
they cultivate various wholesome dhyānas for the sake of attaining happiness in the present life;
they cultivate the pure divine eye for the sake of attaining superior knowledge and vision.
To attain the wisdom of discernment, one cultivates the virtues of the preparatory stages;
to attain the exhaustion of all outflows, one cultivates the diamond-like concentration.
There are four kinds of immeasurables, which serve as antidotes to hatred and the other [afflictions].
Loving-kindness has non-hatred as its nature; compassion is likewise. Joy is joy itself; equanimity is non-attachment.
These aspects follow their respective order: bestowing happiness, removing suffering, sympathetic joy, and impartiality toward sentient beings.
They take sentient beings of the desire realm as their object.
The first two dhyānas are associated with joy; the remaining six are associated with either five or ten [mental factors].
They cannot sever the various afflictions (*kleśa*); when arising in humans, they constitute three types.
There are eight kinds of liberations (*vimokṣa*); the first three have non-attachment (*alobha*) as their nature.
The two types of concentration are each fixed; the four formless concentrations are wholesome;
the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling arises immediately after the "subtle-subtle" mind;
it proceeds from a pure mind of its own level, as well as from an outflowing [attainment] of the lower untainted [level].

Three objects are of the desire realm and are visible; four objects belong to the category of the subsequent classes, the Path, and the Suffering, Origin, and Cessation of the higher realms, as well as non-analytical cessation and space.
There are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); two are like the first liberation.
The next two are like the second [liberation], and the final four are like the third.
There are ten kinds of *kṛtsnāyatana* (totalities): eight are like the pure liberations;
the final two are the pure formless states, taking the four aggregates of their own level as their object.
The attainment of cessation has been explained as before; all others are acquired through both types of acquisition.
The formless attainments depend on the three realms; the others arise only in the human realm.
In the two [lower] realms, one can give rise to the formless attainments by means of causes and karma.
The arising of dhyāna in the form realm is likewise due to the power of the nature of things (*dharmatā*).
The Buddha’s True Dharma is twofold, having the teachings (*śāsana*) and the realization (*adhigama*) as its essence;
when there are those who uphold, explain, and practice it, this [Dharma] abides in the world.
The principles established by the scholars of Kaśmīra, I have for the most part relied upon them to explain the Abhidharma;
wherever there is a slight deficiency in my assessment, that is my own fault, for the determination of the true principles of the Dharma rests with the Muni.
The Great Master, the Eye of the World, has long since closed; those capable of serving as witnesses have mostly perished.
Failing to see the True Dharma and lacking self-restraint, people of base inquiry now throw the Holy Teaching into disorder.
Having personally realized the supreme tranquility, those who upheld his teachings have for the most part passed away;
the world is now without a protector, its manifold virtues lost, and the afflictions roam at will, unrestrained by the hook.
Knowing that the lifespan of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma is gradually perishing as if it had reached one's throat,
and that this is a time when the power of all afflictions increases, one should seek liberation and not be negligent.
